scope: Twenty-first expansion batch: 12 exercises in six matched pairs. Three shared negative-plan/intention-denial answers contrast with three affirmative future intentions. Three past intention denials contrast with three affirmed past intentions, independently of whether the action happened. The first six practice whole basic tsumori patterns; the later six supply dictionary-form verb + tsumori and request only a past ending.

sources.publisher: The Japan Foundation, Nihongo Kyoiku Tsushin; Ichikawa Yasuko
sources.section: つもり（2）: section 1 on an intention recalled as past; section 3 distinguishes V-nai tsumori da, V-ru tsumori wa nai and V-ru tsumori ja/dewa nai, with the latter correcting or qualifying a perceived intention. The final past-negative examples (14)-(16) include a plan not to act, denial of intention despite an unintended effect, and an earlier lack of intention followed by a changed decision. Section 4's V-ta belief/mental-stance negatives were also inspected but are not silently equated with V-ru past-intention denial. Section 3 describes stronger refusal in its repeated-question context; this does not make other negative formulations invalid in the new chosen-negative-plan scenarios.

sources.publisher: The Japan Foundation, Nihongo Kyoiku Tsushin; Ichikawa Yasuko
sources.section: つもり（1）: section 1 compares intention, wish, schedule and decision expressions, qualifies the on-the-spot-decision limitation, and discusses reporting another person's intention. Section 2 distinguishes a V-ta belief from an intention. These are contextual distinctions, not grounds for excluding all alternative intention expressions globally. Some numbered examples are missing from simplified extraction and are not cited.

Actual Verb + tsumori, nai-tsumori, tsumori-datta, ta-tsumori, demonstrative-word apology and Beyond the Basics: tsumori [wa/ga] nai sections. Supports plain verb attachment, negation placement, denial with wa/ga and conversational ja-nakatta. Its emphatic shop-sale refusal and third-person reporting examples are not universal force or person restrictions; they do not prove first-person ga-nai impossible.

Actual About and Caution text: intending not to act versus having no intention to act; wa/ga/ja variants. The absence-of-plan explanation and disinterest nuance differ from the emphatic contexts emphasized by JPF/Tofugu. No universal strength ranking, automatic ga-disinterest implication, or dewa exclusion is adopted; JPF explicitly includes dewa. Inline examples absent from the simplified extraction and the proposed piling-up etymology are not evidence used here.

Exact 売る entry, reading uru, godan verb, sale sense; not its betrayal or provocation senses. Supports the written/kana verb identity and uranai form used in the guitar pair, not automatic naturalness of every completed sentence.
Exact 借りる entry, reading kariru, ichidan verb, borrowing sense; the separate rental and figurative-use senses are not the camera-loan task. Supports the written/kana verb identity and karinai form.

authoringNotes: All scenarios are original. Source patterns do not by themselves attest these exact collocations; require bounded independent linguistic review of all fields and the new explanations.

The first six explicitly practice V-ru tsumori da, V-nai tsumori da and V-ru tsumori wa/ga/dewa/ja nai, with kana tsumori and endings. Their goal is negation placement and intention polarity, not unrestricted production of every intention paraphrase. Accepted alternatives include both negation placements, copular negatives and contractions, not just spelling variants.

The three negative scenarios combine a chosen non-action with correction of another person's assumption: keep the guitar, use one's own camera and keep the existing dictionary. They therefore admit the shared answer class without claiming that every absence of intention entails a deliberate plan of avoidance, or that all denials have identical nuance.

Sell, borrow and buy recur on both sides of the future contrast. The negative model buttons rotate wa-nai, ga-nai and nai-tsumori-da; dewa/ja variants are accepted and explained. One representative correct option does not mean a single acceptable expression; future multi-correct UI work remains separate.

The later six print dictionary-form verb + tsumori, requesting only datta or wa/ga/dewa/ja nakatta. Deleting, moving and discarding recur on both sides. A negative intention can coexist with an actual accidental action; a positive intention can coexist with inability or with successful completion.

The vase's fulfilled plan is deliberate counterevidence to the shortcut that tsumori datta always means failure. The file and receipt obstacles distinguish inability from denied intention. Past completion beliefs with V-ta, double negatives and other endings are outside the explicitly named task, not globally impossible Japanese.

The full linked article inventory was screened. Other intention/decision expressions such as to omou, yotei and koto ni suru do not belong in the explicitly supplied tsumori patterns. Past whole-sentence negative plans may be suitable paraphrases but cannot fit after the printed positive verb + tsumori; the receipt feedback explicitly explains that blank boundary.

The web-search summary supplied real JPF dated citation URLs but also unverified tsumori01/02 URL aliases and conflated parts of V-ta belief negation with V-ru past-intention denial. Only the fetched dated pages and their actual numbered sections/examples are used, not those aliases or the summary's reconstructed quotations.

All269 previous exercise records and identities remain unchanged. The article gains one subsection and one JPF reference bullet, with only the preceding self-assessment transition updated. The source-guide and prior batch records are preserved. One exercise/SRS identity covers its accepted answers and choose/type presentations.
